# Transformers and Motion Forecasting {#ml-transformers .ml-prep}

A car is waiting to turn across a cycle lane. Is the cyclist slowing? Which signal controls this movement? The relevant clues arrive as different kinds of measurements at different places and times. A transformer converts each measurement into a vector and lets the model learn which vectors should exchange information for the prediction at hand.

[Attention by hand](#ml-attention) · [Forecast heads](#ml-forecast-heads) · [Compute cost](#ml-transformer-cost) · [Wayformer](#ml-wayformer) · [MotionLM](#ml-motionlm) · [Scaling laws](#ml-scaling-laws)

## Build a scene out of tokens {#ml-scene-tokens}

A **token** is one unit the network processes. It could represent a cyclist at one instant, an entire short track, or a segment of a lane centerline. For a track point, form a vector containing position, velocity, heading and validity. Represent heading by sine and cosine so that angles just above zero and just below a full turn are close together. Translate positions relative to the target and rotate by its heading. The same approaching cyclist now looks similar at two intersections facing different compass directions. Keep an inverse transform to put predicted paths back on the map.

A learned **embedding** maps each input into a common width \(d\). Include type, time and geometry. Self-attention on a set of otherwise unlabeled vectors has no inherent notion of which came first. Time offsets tell it which observation is newest. Relative positions tell it which lane is beside the cyclist. An encoder may use all valid observations up to the cutoff. A decoder trained to generate the future needs a different visibility rule.

## Compute one attention head by hand {#ml-attention}

For a matrix of \(N\) token rows \(X\), three learned projections produce queries \(Q=XW_Q\), keys \(K=XW_K\), and values \(V=XW_V\). A query describes the information a token seeks. A key describes what another token can be matched on. The value carries the information that will actually be aggregated. With query and key width \(d_k\), compute

\[
P=\operatorname{softmax}_{\mathrm{row}}\!\left(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}+M\right),\qquad Z=PV .
\]

Each row of \(P\) sums to one. \(M\) adds zero to permitted pairs and effectively negative infinity to forbidden ones before normalization. If the number of independent unit-variance terms in a dot product grows, its variance grows too. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps score magnitudes more stable and helps softmax avoid saturating. [Vaswani et al., §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762)

**Work one row.** Give the ego query \(q=(1,0)\), the cyclist key \(k_1=(2,0)\), and the lane key \(k_2=(0,1)\). The scaled scores are \(2/\sqrt2\) and 0. Softmax exponentiates each and divides by their sum, giving weights about 0.804 and 0.196. If the values are \((3,0)\) and \((0,2)\), the output is \((2.412,0.392)\). Masking the cyclist sends all weight to the lane. A large attention weight describes a routing decision inside this head. To test whether the cyclist matters to the final forecast, perturb a plausible feature and measure the change in output.

**Trace the dimensions.** With \(Q,K\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_k}\) and \(V\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_v}\), the score matrix is \(N\times N\) and the result is \(N\times d_v\). In cross-attention, six output queries can attend to \(N\) scene keys, giving a \(6\times N\) score matrix. Multiple heads learn different projections, concatenate their outputs, and mix them with a learned linear layer. A token-wise feedforward network then transforms each row. Residual connections add the input back to a block's output, providing a short gradient path. Layer normalization rescales activations across a token's features. Modern blocks can normalize before the sublayer. The original architecture normalizes after the residual addition. [Vaswani et al., §§3.1–3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762)

## Predict many futures and assign probabilities {#ml-forecast-heads}

A **mixture** head outputs \(K\) candidate paths with probabilities \(\pi_k\) that sum to one. For a Gaussian mixture, each component also predicts a spread. The observed trajectory gets density \(p(y\mid x)=\sum_k\pi_k p_k(y\mid x)\). Minimize the negative log of the **sum** to allow several components to explain the observation. Compute the log-sum with a numerically stable log-sum-exp. Winner-assignment methods instead train one closest component and its classification score. Both designs need a check for collapsed modes, where many output slots predict the same path.

An **autoregressive** decoder factorizes a sequence probability as \(\prod_t p(z_t\mid z_{<t},x)\). A token vocabulary might encode a change in displacement so constant-speed motion is cheap to express. During training, shift targets by one slot and predict each token from earlier recorded ones (**teacher forcing**). A causal mask blocks later tokens. During inference, sample a token, update the history, and repeat. A finer vocabulary reduces rounding error but splits the training data among more classes. Decode recorded token sequences before training to measure the representation's own error floor.

**A leakage test.** The input to predict the third token contains the start symbol and the first two tokens. Replace the fourth target with another legal value. The third prediction should stay identical with randomness disabled. Also shift the third target itself. If its predicted logits change, the decoder saw its label. For synchronous multi-agent decoding, block same-step target tokens for every agent that is supposed to sample in parallel.

## What gets expensive? {#ml-transformer-cost}

At a fixed width, full self-attention forms \(N^2\) score entries per head. Doubling agents and doubling time steps makes \(N\) four times larger if each agent-time pair is a token. The score count grows sixteenfold. An encoder can compress inputs with \(L\) learned latent queries, spending roughly \(LN\) interactions to read the input and \(L^2\) per later latent self-attention layer. An alternative attends along time within each agent and then across agents within each time. With \(A\) agents and \(T\) steps the score count is proportional to \(AT^2+TA^2\). These counts omit projections and memory traffic. Measure latency at realistic scene sizes. [Wayformer, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.05844)

A decoder's key/value cache reuses past projections when tokens arrive sequentially. The next query still attends to the retained history. Measure the cost per generated future under the actual horizon and number of sampled agents. For an interview ablation, hold prediction horizon, hardware, batch size and candidate count fixed. Plot misses on crowded scenes against wall-clock latency. Read the three papers below for contrasting ways to spend that budget.

## Wayformer · How should a forecaster combine maps, signals, and motion? {#ml-wayformer}

**Nayakanti et al., ICRA 2023.** A turning car approaches a crossing. The signal color matters only if it controls that movement. Which part of the model gets to connect the moving car, its lane, and that signal? Wayformer centers and rotates the scene around the target agent, then projects each kind of observation into a vector of the same width. In **early fusion**, all those vectors can exchange information in one encoder. **Late fusion** encodes each input type separately until the decoder. **Hierarchical fusion** adds a shared encoder after the separate ones. [Architecture and training, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.05844)

A learned decoder query acts like a slot for one possible future. Each slot predicts a weight, a path, and uncertainty around the path. Training selects the slot whose mean path is closest to the recorded path. One loss teaches the model to give that slot probability, and another rewards it for assigning high density to the observed positions. Imagine 20 observed left turns and 20 observed right turns. Predicting the mean can put a vehicle on a traffic island. Separate slots can describe both valid paths. [Decoding objective, §3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.05844)

**Read the evidence.** In Table 1's 2021 open motion benchmark, the early-fusion multi-axis latent-query model scores 0.419 mAP against 0.409 for MultiPath++, with six submitted paths. Learned latent queries summarize a long input into fewer vectors before later attention layers. Figure 6 reports 2–16× speedups across the tested fusion configurations. Figure 5 explains a surprise. Separating attention along time and space only reduced measured latency for late fusion. Repeating static road features across time added tokens in the other variants. [Results, Figs. 5–6 and Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.05844)

**Interview drill.** Your prototype has slow predictions at busy intersections. How would you test a smaller latent representation? Hold the training data, output count, and hardware fixed. Sweep the number of queries. Plot p95 latency against miss rate for crowded intersections and check misses on pedestrians separately. A bottleneck could discard a single critical pedestrian while preserving average error. This model predicts one target at a time. Test a separate joint model if the planner needs mutually consistent futures for several agents.

## MotionLM · How can two drivers sample compatible futures? {#ml-motionlm}

**Seff et al., ICCV 2023.** At a narrow entrance, suppose either car can go first, each with probability ½. If exactly one car proceeds, the valid joint futures each have probability ½. Multiplying the individual probability tables incorrectly gives “both proceed” probability ¼. MotionLM builds a shared history of discrete movements. At every timestep it samples each agent's next token given the scene and everyone's *previous* tokens. Agents sample in parallel within that timestep. On the next step, the movement of either car can affect both predictions. [Model factorization, §3.1](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/papers/Seff_MotionLM_Multi-Agent_Motion_Forecasting_as_Language_Modeling_ICCV_2023_paper.pdf#page=3)

A token encodes a quantized change in displacement. Continuing with the previous displacement corresponds to zero change. Thirteen possible values per coordinate produce 169 two-dimensional tokens. During training, the decoder sees recorded history and learns to predict the next recorded token by cross-entropy. During sampling, it consumes its own outputs. Many joint samples are clustered into six weighted alternatives. Clustering whole scenes preserves which car yielded in each sample. [Decoder and aggregation, §§3.2–3.4](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/papers/Seff_MotionLM_Multi-Agent_Motion_Forecasting_as_Language_Modeling_ICCV_2023_paper.pdf#page=4)

**Read the evidence.** Interactive test mAP was 0.2178 for MotionLM and 0.2050 for JFP. JFP had slightly lower joint minADE, 0.8817 m versus 0.8911 m. A best-of-six distance answers whether a close path exists. mAP also depends on how candidates rank. The cleaner test of interaction is the same-family validation comparison. Joint decoding reduced predicted overlap from 0.0404 to 0.0292 relative to marginal decoding. Predicted overlap measures consistency of forecast pairs. It cannot directly estimate collision risk for a deployed planner. [Tables 2–3](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/papers/Seff_MotionLM_Multi-Agent_Motion_Forecasting_as_Language_Modeling_ICCV_2023_paper.pdf#page=7)

**Interview drill.** If the following car accelerates, should the model predict that the lead car will move? Both may be responding to a light. Giving the predictor the follower's complete future can leak the lead car's eventual movement. Table 4 illustrates the trap. Supplying the full conditioning future raises soft mAP to 0.4274, compared with 0.4096 when revealing it over time. To test reactions, branch from identical observed histories, vary only the follower's proposed action, and inspect when the lead car first responds. Even a temporal mask leaves shared hidden causes unresolved. [Conditional rollouts, §4.6 and Table 4](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/papers/Seff_MotionLM_Multi-Agent_Motion_Forecasting_as_Language_Modeling_ICCV_2023_paper.pdf#page=8)

## Scaling Laws of Motion Forecasting and Planning · What should a bigger budget buy? {#ml-scaling-laws}

**Baniodeh et al., 2025 technical report.** Suppose training compute doubles. You can fit a larger network, take more training steps, or split the budget. The authors trained 84 encoder–decoder models from 0.9 to 118 million parameters across seven compute budgets. They used five seconds of history to predict eleven seconds of motion, jointly modeling eight agents. Within each group of runs spending roughly equal compute, they estimated the model size and example count giving the lowest validation loss. [Setup and equal-compute fits, §§2–4](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.08228v1)

**Work the result.** For compute C, the fitted optimal parameter count grows as \(C^{0.63}\) and the optimal number of training examples as \(C^{0.44}\). Doubling compute therefore suggests about 1.55× as many parameters and 1.36× as many examples within this regime. Training examples can come from overlapping windows, so this second number cannot specify how many new miles to collect. Fit uncertainty, architecture, and data composition matter when moving the estimate to another project. [Figs. 3–4 and Eq. 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.08228v1)

**What counts as planning evidence?** The authors fine-tuned the pretrained models on route-conditioned ego plans. In simulation, each decision drew 128 rollouts and executed the first 0.1 seconds of the selected plan before replanning. They calibrated assertiveness across models. Their failure count combined policy-caused collisions with scenarios progressing substantially more or less than the human. Failures fell with pretraining compute in this model family. Separately, the inference study varied raw samples from 8 to 1,024, compressing each set to six reported modes. Sampling a small model more times helped until a larger model became preferable at that inference budget. [Closed-loop protocol and inference curves, §§5.2–6](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.08228v1)

**Interview drill.** A larger model improves log loss, but its planner stalls at unprotected turns. Would you ship it? Start by splitting the composite failure count into collisions, excess progress, and stalls. Compare paired runs from the same initial scenes, including a held-out city, with the same route and response model. Check whether the action selector favors a cautious trajectory even when a suitable turn was sampled. A forecast metric, a sampling budget, and a planner's decision rule each answer a different part of that diagnosis.
